q: Why are carbohydrates, not lipids, the fuel for intense anaerobic exercise?
options: Fatty acids are respired via acetyl groups and the Krebs cycle (O2 needed); glucose can use glycolysis
Lipids can't be stored anywhere in the human body, so none are available during intense exercise
Lipids release less energy per gram than carbohydrates, so they are a poorer fuel
Carbohydrates are respired inside the mitochondria, whereas lipids are respired in the cytoplasm
explanation: Fatty acids are cut into 2C acetyl units in the matrix (β-oxidation, producing NADH and FADH2), which enter the Krebs cycle – both depend on the ETC regenerating NAD+/FAD, so they need O2. Only the small glycerol part can enter glycolysis. Glucose can yield ATP without O2 (glycolysis + lactate) and is mobilised faster because it is water-soluble.
